Q: Removing NULLs caused by GroupBy A:

Use aggregation, but not on all the columns. You can nest the CASE expression in the COUNT(DISTINCT):

SELECT t1.Product, t1.Market, t1.Group1,                                        
        COUNT(DISTINCT t1.ItemID || '-' || t1.Date1) AS StoredMth
        COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN t1.ItemDamagedStatus = 'C' THEN t1.ItemID || '' || t1.Date1) END) AS CompleteDmgMth
        COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN t1.ItemDamagedStatus = 'P' THEN t1.ItemID || '' || t1.Date1 END) AS PartialDmgMth
        COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN t1.ItemDamagedStatus = 'N' THEN t1.ItemID || '-' || t1.Date1 END) AS NotDmgMth
        COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN t1.ItemRepairStatus = 'Y' THEN t1.ItemID || '-' || t1.Date1 END) AS RepairMth
FROM  MainDatabase.Items t1
WHERE  t1.Date1 BETWEEN '2017-01-01' AND '2017-12-31'
GROUP BY t1.Product, t1.Market, t1.Group1;

Q: How to keep OIDC token validation entirely within a central Workspace service when the client registry lives in a separate HIS service (NestJS)? A:

Your question is about OAuth 2.0, not OpenID Connect. Here are a few clarifications on the most central part of your wide-ranging question.

Workspace Backend

This is an authorization server (AS). It issues tokens for authorization that clients send to resource servers. It contains registrations that represent security aspects about trusted clients. It also has access to user attributes and can federate with various identity providers.

Use an industry standard AS and do not build one yourself. E.g. find a Docker based one that you can run for free.

HIS Service

This is a resource server (RS) so should behave like one. Your resource server protects medical resources. It should know nothing about client registrations but can operate on user or client specific medical resources, like appointments.

An RS must validate the access tokens it receives. One way to do so is to make an introspection request to the AS, though it is more common to use JWT validation.

SUMMARY

A medical system should base its security on standards-based documents like those I list here. Using the correct component names makes it easier to understand how they work together.

  • RFC 6749
  • HEART Profile

Q: When does GitHub-flavored markdown render `#«number»` as a rich link? A:

What is the reasoning behind this?

This is mentioned in the "Auto linked references" page from the GitHub documentation, specifically the Issues and pull requests section:

If you reference an issue, pull request, or discussion in a list, the reference will unfurl to show the title and state instead.

As a side note, there are also other possible ways of referencing a specific issue, pull request or discussion that are mentioned:

Reference type Raw reference Short link
Issue or pull request URL https://github.com/jlord/sheetsee.js/issues/26 #26
# and issue or pull request number #26 #26
GH- and issue or pull request number GH-26 GH-26
Username/Repository# and issue or pull request number jlord/sheetsee.js#26 jlord/sheetsee.js#26
Organization_name/Repository# and issue or pull request number github-linguist/linguist#4039 github-linguist/linguist#4039

Q: Select data that isn't NULL A:

GROUP BY with MAX for the other columns:

SELECT a.id,
    MAX(CASE WHEN b.name = 'car' THEN a.value END) AS "Car",
    MAX(CASE WHEN b.boat = 'car' THEN a.value END) AS "Boat" 
WHERE a.id = b.id   
GROUP BY a.id

Q: Lambda Calculus: build a function that takes more arguments with each iteration A:

Another answer here has built this incredibly smart solution by exploiting the intrinsics of Booleans. I can only convince myself in its validity by induction, though have no idea how one could come up with such a non-obvious and downright mysterious approach.

P0 = <T,F>
P1 = <KT,P0> 
OR1 a = P0 a = a T F = a
P2 = <K(KT),P1>
OR2 a b = P1 a b = a (KT) P0 b
                 = a T (P0 b)   = a T b
OR3 a b c = P2 a b c = a (K(KT)) P1 b c
                 = a T (P1 b c) = a T (OR2 b c)
........

This uses the standard K combinator, K = λab.a, and pairs <a,b> = λz.zab such that K a b = a and <a,b> c = c a b.

I would like to find the easy solution here, easy to come up with and easy to understand. You said iteration, you said Church numerals.

First,

TN n a b c ... 
    = n G Z a b c ...              ;; for some G,Z
    = G(G(...(GZ)...)) a b c ...   ;; that should be
  ;;  G r              a      = r
    =   G(...(GZ)...)    b c ...   ;; so G is K
    = K(G(...(GZ)...)) a b c ...   ;; and Z is T
    = K(K(...(KT)...)) a b c ...
    = n K T a b c ...

TN = λn.n K T

is self-evident. The important bit is that Church numerals are folds over implicit lists of ignored elements.

Applying the same exploratory approach,

ORN n a b c ... 
   = G(G(...(GZ)...)) F a b c ...
   =   G(...(GZ)...) (F|a) b c ...
   =    (...(GZ)...) ((F|a)|b) c ...

ORN = λn. n (λrab.r(OR a b)) I F

should be just as self-evident. It is not "smart," but it is simple, self-evidently correct, and demonstrates a standard way to approach such problems in general.

Here again the standard definitions are used, the identity combinator I = λx.x, the Boolean False F = λab.b which is the identity of the OR operation, and whatever the definition of the standard binary OR operation you'd prefer.

Q: Using Python 3.3 in C++ 'python33_d.lib' not found A:

As addition to the answer of @liorda: It might happen that there appears conflicts with other libraries and python. The error C1017: invalid integer constant expression may come up.

For this use @liorda's code and replace

#define _DEBUG

with

#define _DEBUG 1
